summary.text: A 67-year-old man with a past medical history of hypertension was admitted to the ICU with hypoxemic respiratory failure due to severe COVID-19 pneumonitis. He had been admitted to the hospital 2 days earlier with dyspnea and fever for 2 weeks. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein and decreased lymphocytes, SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive, and chest radiography showed bilateral diffuse opacities. He was treated with cefotaxime.

On ICU admission he was intubated with deep sedation, lung-protective ventilation, neuromuscular blockade and intermittent prone ventilation. A CT scan 9 days after ICU admission showed widespread ground-glass opacities and bilateral pulmonary embolisms, for which dalteparin was started. Ten days after ICU admission methylprednisolone was given for 3 days together with empirical antimicrobials, because bronchoalveolar lavage was not possible.

After 4 weeks, sedation was weaned to allow pressure support ventilation, which produced a high respiratory drive with large tidal volumes. Transpulmonary pressure measurement showed a normal dynamic compliance, a plateau pressure of 30 cmH2O, substantial negative esophageal pressures and high transpulmonary pressures, and the patient had no pain, confusion or fear. Sedation was increased and pressure support gradually decreased.

Without respiratory improvement, chest radiography showed a right-sided apical pneumothorax that was not present on an X-ray 3 days earlier. Chest CT confirmed a right-sided ventral pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema up to the left side of the neck and extensive pneumomediastinum, with no airway injury, so barotrauma was considered the most likely cause. Conservative treatment with added antibiotics was chosen, respiratory status gradually improved, and he had a tracheostomy and was weaned off the ventilator.
